interview.question: What is a token in an LLM, why do models use sub-word tokenization, and why should an engineer care about token counts?
interview.model_answer: A token is a sub-word unit produced by the tokenizer; the model reads and generates text one token at a time over a fixed vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens. Sub-word tokenization is the sweet spot between characters (too long, carry little meaning) and whole words (huge vocabulary, out-of-vocabulary problems): it keeps the embedding/output matrices bounded while composing rare words from pieces, so nothing is truly OOV, and it generalizes across languages. Engineers care because tokens are the unit of both cost (you pay per input + output token) and latency (more tokens means more compute and more wall-clock time), and because context windows are measured in tokens. Rough conversions: about 4 English characters per token, 100 tokens is roughly 75 words, and about 1.5 characters per token for Chinese.

sub-word balances char-vs-word tradeoffs and avoids out-of-vocabulary words
~4 chars/token English, 100 tokens ~= 75 words, ~1.5 chars/token Chinese
tokens are the unit of BOTH pricing and latency
context windows / limits are counted in tokens

Ignoring output tokens when estimating cost or latency
Assuming the character-to-token ratio is the same across languages

interview.question: What makes a language model a 'large' language model, and what does 'multi-modal' add?
interview.model_answer: An LLM is a Transformer-based network trained via self-supervised next-token prediction on very large text corpora (web, books, code), typically with hundreds of billions of parameters. 'Large' refers to the combination of massive data and parameter count, which is what unlocks broad, general-purpose ability rather than one narrow task. Multi-modal models extend the same architecture to other modalities, vision (understanding images), image generation, and audio (speech recognition, text-to-speech, realtime voice), usually by encoding those inputs into the same token/embedding space the LLM already uses. Current examples include GPT-5.x, Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.x, Gemini 3.x, and open models like Qwen and GLM.

interview.question: Explain how an LLM generates text. What does 'autoregressive' mean, and where do temperature and top-p fit?
interview.model_answer: The model takes the current sequence, produces a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for the next token, picks one, appends it, and repeats until it emits an end-of-sequence token. 'Autoregressive' means each new token is conditioned on all previously generated tokens, so generation is sequential rather than produced all at once. Temperature and top-p control the sampling step: temperature rescales the distribution (higher = more random, 0 = effectively greedy/deterministic), and top-p (nucleus) samples only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p. Greedy decoding just takes the argmax each step.

generation is inherently sequential

interview.question: Walk me through self-attention. What are Q, K, and V, why the sqrt(d_k) scaling, and why did attention beat RNNs?
interview.model_answer: Each token is projected into a Query, Key, and Value. Attention scores come from the dot product of Queries with Keys, scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k); a softmax turns them into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of the Value vectors, so each token mixes in information from the tokens it attends to. The sqrt(d_k) scaling prevents the dot products from getting large and saturating the softmax (which would kill gradients). Multi-head attention does this several times in parallel. Compared with RNNs, attention gives a constant-length path between any two tokens (better long-range dependencies) and is parallelizable across positions instead of sequential, which is what enabled training at today's scale. Decoders add a causal mask so a token only attends to earlier tokens.

scores = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)); output is a weighted sum of V
sqrt(d_k) scaling stabilizes softmax gradients
captures long-range dependencies via constant path length
parallel across positions vs sequential RNN -> enables scale
multi-head attention + optional causal mask
common_mistakes: Getting confused about which of Q/K/V is summed (it is V, weighted by the QK softmax)
Forgetting the sqrt(d_k) scaling or its purpose

interview.question: Compare encoder-only and decoder-only Transformers. Why is GPT decoder-only and BERT encoder-only, and what do positional encodings do?
interview.model_answer: Both stack identical layers of self-attention plus a feed-forward network with residuals and normalization. Encoder-only models like BERT use bidirectional attention so every token sees the whole sequence, which is ideal for understanding, classification, and embeddings; BERT is pretrained with a masked-language-model objective. Decoder-only models like GPT use causal (masked) attention so a token only sees earlier tokens, which suits autoregressive generation. The original Transformer was encoder-decoder with cross-attention from decoder to encoder (good for translation), but GPT-style models drop the encoder and cross-attention and keep only masked self-attention. Positional encodings supply order information because attention is otherwise permutation-invariant, and they let all positions be processed in parallel during training. Most chat LLMs today are decoder-only.
key_points: stacked identical layers: self-attention + FFN (+ residual/layernorm)
encoder = bidirectional context (BERT); decoder = causal/masked, autoregressive (GPT)
original transformer = encoder-decoder with cross-attention; GPT drops encoder + cross-attention
positional encodings supply order because attention is order-agnostic

interview.question: What is pretraining, why is it called self-supervised, and what do you get at the end of it?
interview.model_answer: Pretraining trains the model to predict the next token over enormous amounts of raw text (web, books, Wikipedia). It is self-supervised because the supervision signal, the next token, already exists in the text, so no human labeling is needed: the model predicts a token, backpropagation compares it to the actual next token, and the weights are updated to reduce the error. The output is a base (foundation) model that has broad knowledge of language, facts, and patterns but is not yet aligned to behave like an assistant; it simply continues text. That is why base models need a further SFT stage (and then RLHF) before they act like ChatGPT.

interview.question: What problem does supervised fine-tuning solve, and how is it different from pretraining?
interview.model_answer: A pretrained base model can continue text but does not reliably follow instructions or act like an assistant. SFT fixes that by training on curated (instruction -> ideal response) pairs, so the model learns to answer questions, follow formats, produce step-by-step solutions, refuse unsafe requests, and stay consistently helpful. It is standard supervised imitation of demonstrations, but on a much smaller, higher-quality dataset than the massive raw corpus used in pretraining. SFT mainly shapes behavior and format rather than injecting large amounts of new knowledge, and it is the step that converts a base model into an instruction-following model.

interview.question: Explain RLHF end to end. Why is it needed after SFT, and what is the role of the reward model?
interview.model_answer: After SFT the model follows instructions but can still be unhelpful, verbose, or unsafe. RLHF aligns it to human preferences: humans compare several candidate responses and rank which is better; those comparisons train a reward model that scores responses, and the LLM is then optimized (classically with PPO) to maximize that reward, i.e., to produce answers people prefer. This improves helpfulness, safety, tone, and honesty beyond what SFT alone achieves. Crucially, humans compare responses rather than authoring them. A modern alternative, DPO, optimizes directly on the preference pairs without training a separate reward model. Risks include reward hacking, sycophancy, and over-optimization.

interview.question: Describe the two phases of LLM inference. What are TTFT and TPOT, and what drives each?
interview.model_answer: Inference splits into prefill and decode. Prefill processes the entire prompt in one parallel pass, populates the KV cache, and emits the first token; the latency to that first token is TTFT and it scales with prompt length. Decode then generates tokens one at a time, each conditioned on all prior tokens, until an EOS token; the per-token cost is TPOT and total generation time scales with the number of output tokens. So total latency is roughly TTFT + TPOT x output_tokens. The KV cache stores past keys and values so attention isn't recomputed every step, which is essential for decode efficiency, and streaming tokens as they are decoded improves perceived latency.

decode: sequential, one token per step -> TPOT, until EOS
total latency ~= TTFT + TPOT x output_tokens
TTFT scales with prompt length; decode time scales with output length
KV cache avoids recomputing attention over past tokens
common_mistakes: Assuming all output tokens are generated in parallel
Ignoring that output length dominates latency for long generations

interview.question: What are emergent abilities in LLMs, and what is the main critique of the concept?
interview.model_answer: Emergent abilities are capabilities that small models essentially can't do (performance near random) but that appear, often sharply, once a model passes a scale threshold in parameters, data, or compute. The Wei et al. 2022 paper showed this for tasks like multi-digit arithmetic, factual QA, multi-task scientific QA, and word-sense disambiguation across models like GPT-3, Gopher, Chinchilla, and PaLM. The main critique (Schaeffer et al.) is that some of these sudden 'jumps' are partly artifacts of choosing discontinuous, exact-match metrics; with smoother metrics the gains look more continuous. Either way, the useful takeaway is that scale can unlock qualitatively new behavior, and things like few-shot and chain-of-thought reasoning mostly emerge in larger models.

driven by scale: parameters, data, compute
examples: multi-digit arithmetic, factual QA, multi-task NLU, word-sense disambiguation

critique: partly a metric artifact (Schaeffer et al.); smoother under continuous metrics

interview.question: Why do LLMs hallucinate, and how would you reduce it in a production system?
interview.model_answer: Hallucination is confident but false or fabricated output. The root cause is that LLMs predict the most likely next token rather than looking up verified facts, so a plausible continuation can be untrue; it is compounded by gaps in training data (the model guesses instead of abstaining) and by the absence of any built-in fact-checker, so it can't distinguish learned facts from invented ones. Stronger, more fluent models make it harder to detect. In production I'd reduce it by grounding responses in retrieved trusted sources (RAG), giving the model tools and requiring citations, lowering temperature for factual tasks, explicitly permitting 'I don't know', and adding verification or self-checking steps. The bamboo-pole example shows why: a fluent answer can still be geometrically wrong (the gate's diagonal is only 5m).

causes: next-token prediction (not fact lookup), training-data gaps, no built-in verifier
harder to detect as models get more fluent and confident
mitigations: RAG/grounding, tools, citations, lower temperature, allow 'I don't know', verification
example: 5.5m pole cannot pass a 4x3 gate whose diagonal is 5m

interview.question: What is prompt engineering, and what are the building blocks of a good prompt?
interview.model_answer: Prompt engineering is the iterative practice of designing prompts that steer the model to do your task well and accurately. A strong prompt typically combines five elements: a clear instruction (what to do), context (relevant background), a role/persona, examples (demonstrations of the task), and, when the task needs reasoning, a chain-of-thought request to work step by step. The practical method is to start simple and then experiment and refine, changing one thing at a time so you can tell what helped. Specificity matters enormously: as the deck's churn example shows, a vague one-liner yields generic output, whereas a prompt that names the audience, features, target roles, pain points, and example lines yields something genuinely usable. It is an empirical loop: measure and iterate.

five elements: instruction, context, role, examples, chain-of-thought
specificity (audience, format, constraints, examples) sharply improves output

common_mistakes: Vague one-line prompts while expecting rich, specific output
Changing many things at once so you can't attribute improvements

interview.question: How do instruction clarity, context, and role each improve a prompt? Give concrete examples.
interview.model_answer: Clarity means removing ambiguity: assume the model doesn't share your unstated context, so spell out what you want, and re-read the prompt as a stranger would, the deck's analogy is briefing a skilled person who doesn't know you. Context supplies background the model needs, such as time/place ('the year 2100 on the Moon'), scenario ('a 10-page deck for a client meeting'), and audience ('explain a neural network to a 5-year-old'), which changes both the content and the level of the answer. Role assigns a persona that shapes tone, personality, and speaking style, can add emotional expression, and can make the model proactively drive the interaction rather than just react. These are concrete instances of the instruction, context, and role elements of a prompt.

role: sets persona/tone/style, adds emotion, can proactively drive interaction

interview.question: What is in-context learning, how does it differ from traditional machine learning, and what do few-shot and zero-shot mean?
interview.model_answer: In-context learning is the ability to condition on examples and instructions placed directly in the prompt and produce the right output for a new query, all within a single forward pass and with no weight update. That is the key difference from classic ML: traditional learning updates parameters from training data and then predicts, whereas ICL 'learns once and forgets next time', the influence lasts only for that context. Few-shot means including a handful of demonstrations in the prompt; zero-shot means giving only the instruction with no examples, and most real prompting is zero-shot (e.g., asking the model to judge a review's sentiment and it correctly detects sarcasm without any labeled examples). ICL is what makes prompt engineering possible and democratizes ML, driving a paradigm shift from task-specific models and training toward general foundation models steered by prompt, context, and harness engineering.

interview.question: What is chain-of-thought prompting, when does it help, and why?
interview.model_answer: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. It helps on multi-step problems, arithmetic, and logic, where a model asked for only the answer often gets it wrong but gets it right when it works through the steps (the paper's tennis-balls / cafeteria-apples example). The deck's explanation is that LLMs are statistical text predictors, not reasoners; CoT doesn't teach reasoning, it elicits and guides it, bridging pieces of knowledge the model already has. It also gives the model more intermediate computation and makes the process inspectable. The catch is that it presupposes the model already knows the basics, and it isn't needed for simple lookups (where it just wastes tokens).

interview.question: What is the difference between prompting a normal model with chain-of-thought and using a dedicated reasoning model?
interview.model_answer: CoT prompting makes any model externalize intermediate steps, but the chain is just the visible form of reasoning, a nice-looking chain can still be fabricated and wrong. A reasoning model is trained and architected specifically to reason: it optimizes the reasoning process itself, not just the appearance of steps, so its internal computation and outputs are closer to rigorous logic and it produces fewer plausible-but-wrong answers. The deck's analogy: a normal model plus CoT 'writes a draft', while a reasoning model 'uses the draft to get the answer right'. In practice reasoning models are trained with large-scale RL on verifiable tasks and spend extra inference-time 'thinking' compute, so you trade latency and cost for accuracy on hard problems.

interview.question: How do a chatbot like ChatGPT, an agentic coding tool like Claude Code, and an autonomous assistant differ, and what does 'orchestrating AI' mean for an engineer's workflow?
interview.model_answer: A chatbot like ChatGPT is a conversational assistant, you exchange messages and it produces text. An agentic coding tool like Claude Code is an LLM wired into a harness with file access, a shell, and tools, so it can take multi-step actions in the actual project (read/edit files, run commands, debug, test), not just reply. An autonomous personal assistant goes further: it runs continuously, often self-hosted, and you drive it via messages to act on your behalf. 'Orchestrating AI' means the engineer's job shifts from hand-writing every line to directing these AI systems, framing tasks, supplying context, and reviewing their actions, which is why the skill set moves toward prompt, context, and harness engineering. Standard setup: Python 3.10+, an agentic coding tool, and Git/GitHub so AI-generated changes stay versioned and reviewable.

interview.question: Why do teams call LLMs through a hosted API instead of running the model themselves, and what are the tradeoffs?
interview.model_answer: A hosted API productizes the model: the provider handles inference, GPU scheduling, scaling, and uptime, so the application only owns business logic and can ship AI features quickly. It also gives a unified abstraction -- model, messages, role, temperature -- that is similar across providers, so integration and switching are cheap. The tradeoffs are less control over the model, data leaving your environment, ongoing per-token cost, rate limits, and dependency on the vendor's availability. When data privacy or total control matters, teams self-host open models (e.g. vLLM) instead.

interview.question: You need a production LLM setup that survives a provider outage and lets you swap models. What architecture and tools do you use?
interview.model_answer: Put a routing/gateway layer between the app and the models rather than calling one provider directly. An aggregator like OpenRouter gives a unified API to many models with automatic fallback if a provider is down. An enterprise gateway like LiteLLM or Portkey standardizes everything to OpenAI-style syntax, load-balances across multiple keys and endpoints, and enforces rate limits, auth, and usage tracking. If data privacy or full control is required, self-host open or fine-tuned models with an engine like vLLM. The app codes against one stable interface, and reliability/cost/observability live in the gateway.

interview.question: How do you manage an LLM API key across local dev and production without leaking it?
interview.model_answer: Never hard-code the key or commit it. Locally, either export it as an environment variable (the OpenAI SDK reads OPENAI_API_KEY automatically) or keep it in a .env file loaded with python-dotenv, with .env added to .gitignore so it never reaches source control. In production, store it in a secrets manager like AWS Secrets Manager and inject it at runtime, rotate it periodically, and scope keys per environment/service. Treat the key like a password -- OpenAI only shows the full secret once at creation, so if it leaks you rotate immediately.

interview.question: Walk through a basic Chat Completion API call. What are the required pieces and where is the model's answer?

interview.question: Explain how temperature affects LLM sampling. What does temperature 0 versus a high temperature do, and mathematically why?
interview.model_answer: The model outputs a logit per vocabulary token; softmax converts logits to probabilities and the next token is sampled from that distribution. Temperature T divides the logits before softmax. As T -> 0 the largest logit dominates, so the distribution collapses onto the top token and output becomes near-deterministic (greedy) -- ideal for extraction, classification, or code where you want consistency. As T grows, logits are squashed together so the distribution flattens toward uniform, increasing randomness and, at extreme values, producing gibberish. T=1 uses the model's natural distribution. So temperature trades determinism/consistency against diversity/creativity.
key_points: logits -> softmax -> probability distribution -> sample the next token
temperature divides logits before softmax: exp(logit/T)
T->0 sharpens to the top token (near-deterministic); high T flattens toward uniform
low T for factual/structured, higher T for creative

Confusing temperature (rescales the whole distribution) with top-p (truncates the tail)

interview.question: What is top-p (nucleus) sampling and how does it differ from temperature? Why not tune both at once?
interview.model_answer: Top-p keeps the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p and samples only from that nucleus, discarding the long low-probability tail. The set size is dynamic: when the model is confident the nucleus is tiny, when it is uncertain it grows. Temperature instead rescales the entire distribution's sharpness without cutting any tokens. They control different things -- truncation vs. sharpening -- and interact, so the standard advice is to adjust one and leave the other at its default; tuning both makes the combined effect hard to predict and reproduce.
key_points: nucleus = smallest set of top tokens whose cumulative prob >= p, then sample from it
nucleus size adapts to model confidence
top-p truncates the tail; temperature rescales the whole distribution
recommended: change temperature OR top_p, not both
common_mistakes: Describing top-p as a fixed number of tokens (that's top-k)
Cranking both temperature and top_p together and getting unpredictable output
followups: How does top-p differ from top-k?
For a JSON-extraction task, would you raise or lower these, and why?

interview.question: What is streaming in an LLM API, why is it used, and how does the response shape change when you enable it?
interview.model_answer: Streaming sends the completion token-by-token as it is generated instead of after the full response is ready. Since generation is autoregressive (predict next token), partial output exists immediately, so streaming cuts perceived latency and improves UX -- the user sees text appear right away. It's delivered over Server-Sent Events: one long-lived HTTP connection over which the server pushes events, lightweight and one-directional. In code you pass stream=True and iterate the response; each chunk carries a delta at choices[0].delta.content that you accumulate, rather than a single choices[0].message.content.
key_points: streams partial tokens as generated -> lower perceived latency, better UX
enabled by autoregressive next-token generation
transport is SSE: single long HTTP connection, server pushes events
stream=True; read choices[0].delta.content per chunk, not message.content
common_mistakes: Reading message.content on a streamed response instead of delta.content
Confusing SSE (one-way server push) with bidirectional WebSockets
followups: How do you accumulate a full message and detect the end of the stream?

interview.question: Why is asyncio a good fit for calling LLM APIs, and when would it NOT help? Contrast it with multi-threading.
interview.model_answer: LLM calls are I/O-bound -- most of the time is spent waiting on the network. asyncio runs many such calls concurrently on a single thread using an event loop and cooperative scheduling: a coroutine hits `await` on a network call, yields control, and the loop runs other coroutines until the response returns. That scales to thousands of concurrent connections with far less memory and overhead than spawning OS threads, and it sidesteps the race conditions of shared-state threading. It does NOT help CPU-bound work: because of the GIL and single-threaded execution, heavy computation still blocks the loop -- for that you use multiprocessing or native/vectorized code. Multi-threading also can't accelerate CPU-bound Python (GIL) but is useful for blocking libraries that release the GIL; async is preferred for high-concurrency I/O.
key_points: GIL: one thread runs Python at a time; lock released during I/O
asyncio = single-thread event loop + cooperative multitasking
coroutine suspends/yields via async/await without blocking
great for high-concurrency I/O (LLM calls); bad for CPU-bound work
AsyncOpenAI + await + asyncio.gather to run calls concurrently
common_mistakes: Expecting asyncio to speed up CPU-heavy computation
Blocking the event loop with a synchronous call inside a coroutine
Forgetting to await a coroutine (it just returns a coroutine object)
followups: How does asyncio.gather differ from awaiting calls one by one?

interview.question: What are the system, user, and assistant roles in a chat API, and what belongs in each?
interview.model_answer: Messages are role-tagged. The system role sets durable behavior -- the model's role, instructions, background, audience, goal, tone, output format, constraints, and few-shot examples -- and applies across the conversation. The user role carries the specific request for the current turn. The assistant role is the model's own replies, which you also include when replaying history so the model has context. The design pattern is a rich, reusable system prompt plus a short, variable user message, which keeps a single well-crafted instruction set working across many different user inputs and makes prompts easier to maintain and test.
key_points: system = role/instructions/tone/format/constraints/few-shot; durable contract
user = the request for this turn
assistant = model replies and replayed history
rich reusable system prompt + short user message
common_mistakes: Dumping everything into the user message and leaving system empty
Putting per-request variable content into the system prompt
followups: Where do few-shot examples go, system or user?
How does the assistant role enable multi-turn memory?

interview.question: Compare raw strings, string concatenation, and string templates for building prompts. Which do you use and why?
interview.model_answer: A raw string is a single hard-coded blob -- quick but not modular or reusable. String concatenation stitches variables together but obscures the overall structure and makes it easy to lose separators or spaces. String templates -- a fixed skeleton with named placeholders filled via str.format (or f-strings / a templating library) -- are the best default: the structure stays visible, the fixed wording is separated from the variable values, and you can fill the same template with different inputs reliably. In production this makes prompts readable, versionable, and testable, and it's how you'd back a template that takes user-supplied fields at runtime.
key_points: raw string: not modularized
concatenation: structure hard to see, separator bugs
template + str.format: structure visible, fixed vs. variable separated, reusable
templates are the production-friendly choice

Hard-coding values that should be template variables
followups: When would you reach for Jinja2 or a prompt-template library over str.format?

interview.question: Why ask an LLM for structured JSON with a schema instead of parsing free text, and how do JSON mode and a JSON schema differ?
interview.model_answer: Applications need to consume the output programmatically, and parsing free-form text is brittle -- phrasing varies and regex/heuristics break. Asking for JSON makes the output machine-readable. Plain JSON mode guarantees the response is syntactically valid JSON but not its shape, so fields can be missing or mistyped. Supplying a JSON Schema (with strict on) constrains the model to your exact structure -- required keys, types, no extra properties -- so you can json.loads it and rely on the fields directly. That removes a class of runtime errors and is essential when the output feeds a downstream function, database, or tool. It's also the same schema mechanism underlying function/tool calling.
key_points: structured output is reliably parseable vs. brittle free-text parsing
JSON mode: valid JSON, shape not guaranteed
json_schema + strict: enforces field names, types, required, no extra props

Not validating the parsed object before using it

interview.question: LLMs are stateless -- so how does a chatbot 'remember' earlier turns, and what problem does that create as the conversation grows?
interview.model_answer: The model has no memory between calls; it only sees the tokens in the current request's context window (system prompt + history + retrieved data + current message). To simulate memory you append each user message and each assistant reply to the messages list and resend the entire conversation every turn. The cost is that input tokens grow with the conversation, raising latency and price, and once you exceed the context window older content gets truncated and effectively forgotten. Mitigations include trimming old turns, summarizing history into a compact form, or retrieving only the relevant prior context (RAG) instead of resending everything.
key_points: context window = input + output tokens per request
model is stateless -> resend all relevant context each turn
output tokens become next turn's input; history appended to messages
growing history costs tokens/latency; over-limit content is truncated
mitigate via trimming, summarization, retrieval
common_mistakes: Assuming the API remembers previous calls automatically
Never trimming history until you blow past the context limit
followups: How would you keep a long chat within the context window?

interview.question: Walk through the function/tool-calling loop end to end. Who actually executes the function?
interview.model_answer: You pass the model a list of tool definitions (name, description, JSON-schema parameters) alongside the user request. If the model decides a tool is needed, it returns a tool call -- the chosen tool name plus structured JSON arguments -- but it does not execute anything. Your application runtime parses those arguments, runs the real function, and gets structured data back. You then append the assistant's tool-call message and a tool message carrying the result (keyed by tool_call_id) to the conversation and call the model again; it reads the result and produces the final natural-language answer. The key point: the model only selects the tool and emits arguments; the runtime performs the action and returns the result as context.
key_points: model chooses a tool and emits structured arguments; it does NOT run it
the application/runtime executes the function
5 steps: define+ask -> tool call -> execute -> return result as context -> final answer
result is fed back as a tool message (tool_call_id) with full prior history

Not sending the tool result back, so the model can't produce a grounded final answer
Dropping prior messages when sending the tool result
followups: How do you handle multiple or parallel tool calls in one turn?

interview.question: A model keeps calling the wrong tool or filling arguments badly. Before blaming the model, what do you fix?
interview.model_answer: Tool-selection quality is driven mostly by the tool definitions, not raw model intelligence, so I fix the definitions first. Each function should have a narrow, single purpose, clear and descriptive parameter names, and no ambiguous overlap with other tools. I'd tighten the description to say exactly when to use (and not use) the tool, give every parameter a precise type and description in the JSON schema, and split broad or overlapping tools into focused ones so the model isn't guessing between near-duplicates. Good few-shot examples and required-field constraints help too. Only after the definitions are clean would I consider model or prompt changes.
key_points: tool choice is shaped by the definition, not mainly 'model intelligence'
narrow single purpose, clear parameter names, no ambiguous overlap
precise descriptions + JSON-schema types drive correct selection and arguments
split broad/overlapping tools into focused ones

One catch-all tool with an 'action' string instead of distinct focused tools
Cryptic parameter names with no descriptions
followups: How would you disambiguate two tools that could both apply?

interview.question: How does the Anthropic Messages API differ from OpenAI's Chat Completions API, and what other OpenAI APIs would you reach for beyond chat?
interview.model_answer: The concepts are the same -- a model, a list of role-tagged messages, temperature -- but the surfaces differ. In Anthropic's client.messages.create, max_tokens is required, the system prompt is a top-level system= parameter rather than a message with role 'system', and you read the reply from response.content[0].text instead of choices[0].message.content. Because providers share the core abstraction, porting between them is mostly mechanical. Beyond chat, OpenAI offers the Embedding API (vectors for semantic search and RAG), Audio API (STT/TTS), Images API (generation/editing), and Moderation API (safety), which you compose with chat to build real applications. Model ids like claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 are dated, so I'd pin a current model and keep the call shape.

read text from response.content[0].text (vs. choices[0].message.content)

interview.question: Why would you add RAG to an LLM instead of just fine-tuning it or relying on a bigger context window?
interview.model_answer: A bare LLM has three gaps RAG closes. First, knowledge cutoff: weights are frozen at training time, so it can't know today's facts or anything published after the cutoff. Second, private data: your enterprise documents and customer data were never in training, so the model literally cannot answer questions about them. Third, context and cost: even million-token windows can't hold a whole corpus, and stuffing everything in hurts quality (the model gets distracted / loses information in the middle) and burns tokens. RAG retrieves just the relevant, current, private passages and injects them at query time. Fine-tuning teaches style/behavior and bakes in knowledge that goes stale and is hard to update or attribute; RAG keeps knowledge external, freshly updatable, and citable, which is why it's the default for grounding on changing or proprietary data.
key_points: Knowledge cutoff: frozen weights, no fresh facts
Private/domain data absent from training
Context windows can't hold a whole corpus; stuffing hurts quality and cost
RAG injects relevant evidence at query time
RAG vs fine-tuning: external, updatable, citable knowledge
common_mistakes: Assuming a bigger context window removes the need for retrieval
Thinking fine-tuning is how you add fresh/private facts

interview.question: In one or two sentences, what is RAG, and what are its two stages?
interview.model_answer: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) means retrieving relevant information first and then asking the LLM to answer grounded in that information. It has two stages: retrieval — a search problem that finds the right passages from documents, databases, or other sources — and generation, where the LLM reads those passages and produces a grounded, citable answer. The key insight is that retrieval quality bounds answer quality: if the relevant evidence isn't retrieved and formatted into the context window, the model can't use it, so most of the engineering is in the retrieval half.
key_points: Retrieve-then-generate two-stage pattern
Retrieval is a search problem; generation is grounded reasoning
Format evidence into the context window
Retrieval quality caps answer quality
Perplexity-style search assistant as an example
common_mistakes: Describing RAG as only 'embeddings + vector DB' (retrieval is broader)
Focusing all effort on the LLM prompt and neglecting retrieval quality
followups: What are the failure modes when retrieval returns the wrong passage?

interview.question: How do you structure the prompt/context window for a RAG call, and why treat retrieved passages as untrusted?
interview.model_answer: Put instructions in the system prompt, the user's question in the user turn, and the retrieved passages after the question as a tool result or a clearly delimited context block, then tell the model to answer using only that evidence and to say when it's insufficient. The passages must be treated as untrusted data, not instructions, because they come from documents you don't fully control: a retrieved chunk could contain 'ignore previous instructions and...' — an indirect prompt injection. Defenses include clearly labeling the block as source-only material, keeping instructions in the system prompt where injected text can't easily override them, and never executing actions purely on the basis of retrieved text. Attaching source and date metadata per document also enables citation and lets the model prefer the current policy over a stale one.

Answer using only retrieved evidence; admit when insufficient
Retrieved content is untrusted data, not instruction (indirect prompt injection)
Per-doc source/date metadata enables citation and recency preference
common_mistakes: Concatenating retrieved text inline with no delimiter or trust boundary
Letting retrieved text act as instructions (prompt-injection risk)
Not asking the model to abstain when evidence is missing (invites hallucination)

interview.question: Walk me through the architecture of a production RAG system, offline vs online.
interview.model_answer: There are two paths. Offline indexing runs when data changes: pull from data sources, load and clean, chunk into passages, embed each chunk, and index/store them — usually a vector database for the embeddings plus a metadata/document store for the raw text and filterable fields. Online serving runs per request: take the user query, process it (rewrite, expand, or route it), retrieve candidates — semantic, keyword, SQL, or graph, often several combined — rerank the merged candidates, build the context window from the top passages, call the LLM, and return the answer. The separation matters because the expensive work (chunking, embedding, indexing) is amortized offline so queries stay fast, and the retrieve->rerank split lets you fetch broad recall cheaply then rank precisely.

Store = vector DB (embeddings) + metadata/docs (raw text, filters)
Online: query -> query processing -> retrieve -> rerank -> build context -> LLM -> answer
Retrieve can be semantic/keyword/SQL/graph, often combined
Retrieve (recall) then rerank (precision) two-phase pattern

Assuming retrieval is only vector search
Skipping reranking and feeding raw top-k semantic hits straight to the LLM

interview.question: RAG isn't just vector search — what data sources and retrieval methods should a strong RAG system support?
interview.model_answer: Match the method to the data and the intent. Unstructured text (PDFs, wikis, help docs) is served by embedding (semantic) search and keyword search. Structured data in databases or analytics platforms is served by SQL or database queries — you don't embed a numeric table to answer 'what was Q3 revenue'. Semi-structured data like JSON, markdown, and logs uses parsing plus field/keyword queries. Graph data like a knowledge graph uses graph queries for multi-hop relations. Beyond stored data, tools/APIs/MCPs fetch live or computed results, and memory (history, preferences) is retrieved to personalize. The takeaway is that retrieval is a routing problem: pick or combine methods based on data shape and query type, and expose them as tools an agent can choose.

Structured data -> SQL / DB queries
Semi-structured (JSON/markdown/logs) -> parsing + field/keyword
Graph data -> graph queries; multi-hop relations
Tools/APIs/MCPs and memory as retrieval sources
Choose method by data shape and query intent (routing)

interview.question: How does BM25 keyword retrieval work, what is an inverted index, and where does lexical search fail?
interview.model_answer: BM25 is a bag-of-words ranking function that scores a document by term frequency (more occurrences of the query terms is better, with diminishing returns), inverse document frequency (rarer terms are more discriminative and weigh more), and document-length normalization so long documents don't get an unfair edge. It's powered by an inverted index, a map from each term to the postings list of documents containing it, so at query time you union small postings lists instead of scanning the whole corpus — that's what makes it fast. Lexical search shines on exact identifiers, error codes, and code symbols, and it's transparent. Its weakness is semantic recall: it matches surface tokens, so 'reimbursement' misses 'expense claim', and it can flood you with matches that need ranking. That vocabulary-mismatch gap is exactly why teams add embedding search or go hybrid.

BM25 = term frequency + inverse document frequency + length normalization
Inverted index maps term -> postings list of documents
Fast because you look up pre-built mappings, not scan every doc
Great for exact IDs/codes; weak on synonyms/paraphrase (vocabulary mismatch)

interview.question: Compare semantic (embedding) and keyword search. Why do production RAG systems usually go hybrid?
interview.model_answer: Embedding search retrieves by meaning in a shared vector space, so it handles synonyms and paraphrase — 'get reimbursed for travel' matches 'expense claim' with no shared words. Its weaknesses are weak exact matching (it blurs identifiers, codes, versions) and that 'similar' isn't 'correct' — it can surface plausible but wrong chunks. Keyword/BM25 is the opposite: precise on exact tokens but blind to synonyms (vocabulary mismatch). Because the failure modes are complementary, hybrid retrieval runs both and fuses the results — typically Reciprocal Rank Fusion or a weighted blend — then reranks the top candidates. You get lexical precision on exact terms plus semantic recall on paraphrases, which consistently beats either method alone, and a reranker cleans up the merged list before it hits the context window.

Embedding weaknesses: weak exact match; similar != correct
Keyword is precise on tokens, blind to synonyms
Hybrid = BM25 + vector, fused (e.g. RRF) then reranked
Complementary failure modes -> hybrid usually wins

interview.question: What is an embedding, and how do you choose a text-embedding model?
interview.model_answer: An embedding is a fixed-length numeric vector from a learned model that maps unstructured data — text, images, audio — into a space where geometric closeness means semantic similarity; that's why you can search by meaning. Word embeddings show it clearly: related words and their inflected forms cluster together in 2-D projections. Modern sentence/passage embedding models (OpenAI, Qwen, Voyage, BGE, Sentence Transformers) extend this to whole texts so paraphrases land nearby. To choose one I benchmark on the MTEB leaderboard and, more importantly, on my own domain data, weighing retrieval quality, dimensionality (storage and search latency), max sequence length versus my chunk size, multilingual needs, and cost/hosting (managed API vs open-weight self-hosted). Two disciplines: embed queries and documents with the same model, and re-embed the whole corpus if you change models, since vectors from different models aren't comparable.

Similar meaning -> nearby vectors (word embeddings cluster related words)
Models: OpenAI, Qwen, Voyage, BGE, Sentence Transformers
Compare on MTEB leaderboard + your own domain

interview.question: What is cosine similarity, how does it relate to the dot product, and why normalize embeddings?
interview.model_answer: Cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between two vectors: dot(a,b) divided by the product of their norms. It measures direction and ignores magnitude, which is what you want for text embeddings because meaning is encoded in orientation, not length. It relates to the dot product directly — cosine is just the dot product of the length-normalized vectors — so if you L2-normalize every embedding to unit length up front, cosine similarity equals the raw dot product. That's the practical win: ranking neighbors becomes one big matrix multiply (query dot all documents), which is extremely fast. Cosine ranges from -1 to 1. Euclidean distance is an alternative but is magnitude-sensitive, and Hamming distance applies to binary/hash codes.

Normalize to unit length -> cosine == dot product
Enables fast top-k via a single matrix multiply

interview.question: How do you implement exact k-NN retrieval over embeddings with numpy, and what's its cost?
interview.model_answer: Stack the document vectors into a matrix and take the dot product of the query against all of them in one call — np.dot(query, docs) gives a similarity score per document — then np.argmax for the single best or np.argsort/np.argpartition for the top-k. It's fast in numpy because the matmul is vectorized and runs on optimized BLAS/MKL kernels rather than a Python loop. Two things to get right: the dot product equals cosine similarity only if the vectors are L2-normalized, and the document matrix has to be oriented so the product broadcasts (docs as rows). The catch is cost: exact KNN is a brute-force linear scan, O(N*d) per query, comparing against every vector. That's fine for thousands to low millions of vectors but doesn't scale, which is why large systems switch to approximate nearest neighbor with an index.

np.dot(query, docs) scores all docs at once; np.argmax for best
top-k via np.argsort / np.argpartition
Fast due to vectorization + BLAS/MKL
dot == cosine only if normalized
Exact KNN is O(N*d) brute force -> motivates ANN

interview.question: What is Approximate Nearest Neighbor search, why is it needed, and how do you evaluate an ANN index?
interview.model_answer: ANN finds vectors that are close enough to the query far faster than exact search. Exact KNN scans every vector, O(N) per query, which collapses at millions or billions of vectors. ANN builds an index offline so a query only explores a small candidate subset instead of the whole set, trading a little accuracy for a big speedup. Because it's approximate, the key metric is recall@k — the fraction of true nearest neighbors it returns — traded against queries-per-second and memory footprint; you pick an operating point on that curve for your latency SLA and scale. Common algorithms are HNSW (graph), LSH (hashing), and IVF-style partitioning, available in libraries like FAISS and ScaNN, and ann-benchmarks.com plots their recall-vs-throughput so you can compare implementations empirically.

ANN builds an index; explores a promising subset; approximate results
Trades a little accuracy for much better speed
Evaluate with recall@k vs QPS vs memory
Algorithms/libs: HNSW, LSH, FAISS, ScaNN; benchmarks at ann-benchmarks.com

interview.question: Explain how HNSW works. What do the hierarchy and the 'navigable small world' graph each contribute?
interview.model_answer: HNSW is a graph-based ANN index. The base idea is a navigable small-world graph: each vector is a node linked to a few near neighbors, and because it's a small-world graph any two nodes are a few hops apart. Search is greedy — start at an entry point and keep moving to the neighbor closest to the query until no neighbor is closer — so you never scan all vectors. The 'hierarchical' part stacks this into layers: sparse top layers with long-range links let you take big steps to cross the space fast, and dense lower layers with short links let you refine precisely. A query enters at the top, greedily descends coarse-to-fine using each layer's best node as the entry to the next, and finishes on the dense bottom layer. That gives about logarithmic search with high recall. The tradeoffs are that the graph sits in RAM and is costlier to build/update, and you tune M (neighbors per node) and efSearch (query breadth) to move along the recall-vs-latency curve.

Greedy search: move to the neighbor closest to the query, no full scan
Hierarchy: sparse top layers = big steps; dense bottom layers = small steps
Descend coarse-to-fine, entry point carried down between layers

interview.question: What does a vector database give you beyond a raw ANN library like FAISS, and how would you choose one?
interview.model_answer: A vector database wraps an ANN index (often HNSW) with everything you need in production. On top of similarity search it adds metadata storage with filtered search — so you can constrain a vector query by tenant, date, or permissions — plus CRUD/upserts and deletes, persistence and durability, horizontal scaling/sharding, and usually hybrid search that fuses vector and keyword ranking. A raw library like FAISS gives you fast search but you'd build all of that yourself. Options include purpose-built stores like Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, and Chroma, and search engines that added vectors like Elasticsearch and Vespa. I'd choose based on managed vs self-hosted, scale/latency targets, quality of metadata filtering and hybrid search, how often data changes (update/delete support), and whether I already operate a search engine I can extend instead of adopting a new system.

interview.question: What are the main failure modes of naive RAG, and which optimization technique addresses each?
interview.model_answer: Three big ones. Wrong retrieval: the retriever returns an off-target or stale passage — like answering a 2026-policy question with the 2022 policy — fixed with better queries (query transformation / HyDE), hybrid retrieval and reranking, and recency/metadata filtering. Missing context: the retrieved chunk is relevant but incomplete because the conditions or reasons live in another section that wasn't retrieved — a chunking problem — fixed with small-to-big retrieval (embed small, feed the expanded parent) and hierarchical retrieval. No multi-step reasoning: single-shot retrieval can't answer questions that need several sources joined, like whether churn rose after a release, which needs release notes plus tickets plus metrics — fixed with agentic RAG that plans, issues multiple retrievals, and decides when it has enough. Diagnosing which failure you have tells you which technique to reach for.
key_points: Wrong retrieval (off-target/stale) -> query transformation, hybrid+rerank, recency filter
Missing context (incomplete chunk) -> small-to-big, hierarchical retrieval; a chunking problem
No multi-step reasoning (needs joined sources) -> agentic RAG
Map the observed failure to the right technique
common_mistakes: Blaming the LLM when the real problem is retrieval or chunking
Applying one fix (e.g. bigger model) to all failure modes

interview.question: Explain small-to-big retrieval and HyDE. What problem does each solve?
interview.model_answer: Small-to-big decouples the retrieval unit from the generation unit: you embed and search over small units like a sentence or short chunk for precise matching, but when you build the prompt you hand the LLM the expanded surrounding text — the parent paragraph or document. Small chunks retrieve sharply while the expanded window restores the context the model needs to answer, which fixes the 'missing context' failure where a tiny chunk is a great match but unreadable alone. HyDE — Hypothetical Document Embeddings — is a query transformation for the asymmetry between a short question and a long answer passage: it asks an LLM to draft a hypothetical answer to the query, even if not fully correct, then embeds that draft and retrieves with its vector. A hypothetical answer resembles real answer passages far more than the raw question does, so recall improves and it generalizes across phrasings and languages. The costs are an extra LLM call and latency, and risk if the hypothetical is badly off.
key_points: Small-to-big: embed/search small units, feed expanded parent text to the LLM
Decouples retrieval unit from generation unit; fixes missing context
HyDE: LLM writes a hypothetical answer, embed IT, retrieve with its vector
Bridges question-vs-answer embedding asymmetry; improves recall
HyDE cost: extra LLM call/latency; can drift if hypothetical is wrong
common_mistakes: Embedding and generating over the same large chunk (loses precision or context)

interview.question: What are hierarchical retrieval and agentic RAG, and when do you reach for each?
interview.model_answer: Hierarchical retrieval organizes the corpus as summaries over raw chunks and retrieves recursively: first match the query against document-level summaries to pick the right document(s), then descend into that document's raw chunks — often with metadata filters — to get the exact passages. It shrinks the search space before going fine, so it improves precision and cuts cross-document noise on large multi-document corpora. Agentic RAG replaces fixed single-shot retrieval with an LLM agent that loops: it repeatedly asks whether it has enough information, and if not it picks a source — vector DB, web search, or a tool/API like Slack or GitHub — retrieves more, and only generates once it's satisfied. That planning-and-tool-selection loop is what enables multi-step questions that need several sources joined, like whether churn rose after a release. I reach for hierarchical retrieval when the corpus is large and multi-document, and for agentic RAG when questions need multi-hop reasoning or multiple tools — accepting the extra latency, cost, and the need to bound the loop.
key_points: Hierarchical: summaries over raw chunks; retrieve coarse summary then recurse into chunks
Metadata filtering narrows within a document; cuts cross-document noise
Agentic RAG: LLM agent loops, 'do I have enough data?', picks sources/tools, then answers
Agentic fixes multi-step reasoning; sources include vector DB, web search, tools/APIs
Tradeoffs: more LLM calls, latency/cost, must bound the loop and handle tool errors

Making everything agentic when a single retrieval would do (needless cost/latency)

interview.question: What is the difference between using an LLM through prompting versus building an AI workflow?
interview.model_answer: Prompt-based use is ad-hoc, conversational usage where a human asks and the model responds, and the human drives each step - great for drafting, brainstorming, summarizing, and quick analysis. An AI workflow embeds the model into a structured, predefined sequence of steps that the developer orchestrates in code, so it runs the same way every time. The core distinction is who controls the control flow: the human in prompting, versus fixed code in a workflow. You move to a workflow when a task is repeatable and has predictable inputs and outputs and you want consistency and reliability.

prompt-based is best for drafting/brainstorming/summarizing/quick analysis

interview.question: Why is classic RAG considered a workflow rather than an agent, and what would make it agentic?
interview.model_answer: Classic RAG follows a fixed, predefined pipeline: the user asks, the system forms one or more queries, retrieves relevant chunks, builds a prompt, and the model generates an answer. The control flow is hardcoded and the LLM only fills specific slots (query generation and final answer), so it is a workflow. It becomes agentic RAG when the model itself decides the control flow - whether to retrieve at all, how many retrieval rounds to run, how to rewrite queries after seeing weak results, and when it has gathered enough context. In agentic RAG retrieval is a tool the model calls in a reasoning loop rather than a fixed step.

AI plays roles in one or more components, not overall control flow

interview.question: How do you decide between a single prompt, a workflow, and an agent for an LLM application?
interview.model_answer: I follow the 'simplest thing that works' principle from Anthropic's Building Effective Agents. Start with a single prompt; if the task needs several coordinated, well-defined steps with predictable inputs and outputs, use a workflow because it gives predictability and consistency. Only escalate to an autonomous agent when the problem is open-ended - you can't predict the number of steps or hardcode the path. Each step up the ladder buys flexibility but costs latency, token spend, and debuggability, and reduces determinism, so I add complexity only when the task genuinely requires it.

workflows give predictability & consistency for well-defined tasks

more autonomy costs latency, tokens, determinism, debuggability

interview.question: Name and contrast the common LLM workflow patterns (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, evaluator-optimizer).
interview.model_answer: Prompt chaining decomposes a task into an ordered sequence where each call consumes the previous output, often with a programmatic gate between steps to catch bad intermediates - good for tasks with clean subtasks like outline-then-draft or generate-then-translate. Routing classifies the input and sends it to a specialized branch - e.g. different customer-service intents, or cheap models for easy questions and capable models for hard ones. Parallelization fires several calls at once and aggregates them with a synthesizer - e.g. reading many pages concurrently, or multiple independent code-vulnerability reviewers (sectioning or voting). Evaluator-optimizer pairs a generator with an evaluator that gives feedback in a loop until the output is accepted - e.g. draft-and-review document editing. All four are workflows: the developer hardcodes the control flow and the LLM fills the steps, unlike an agent that chooses its own path.
key_points: prompt chaining = sequential steps, each consumes prior output; optional gate/check
routing = classify input, dispatch to a specialized branch (incl. model-tier routing)
parallelization = concurrent calls aggregated by a synthesizer (sectioning/voting)
evaluator-optimizer = generator + evaluator feedback loop until accepted
all are fixed orchestrations (developer-defined), not agents

interview.question: What are your options for implementing an AI workflow, and how do code-first frameworks compare to visual builders?
interview.model_answer: You can build workflows code-first with a framework like LangChain, expressing the chain of LLM calls, tools, and retrieval in code, or visually with a low-code platform like Dify.ai, which offers a drag-and-drop UI. Code-first gives you full control, testability, and version control and fits complex or production systems, but costs engineering time. Visual builders let you prototype and let non-engineers assemble workflows fast, which is great for iteration and simple pipelines, but they can be harder to customize deeply or integrate into a rigorous CI/testing setup. I pick based on team skills, how custom the logic is, and whether it's a prototype or a production system.

interview.question: What are the main challenges of AI workflows, and how do they show up in a RAG pipeline?
interview.model_answer: Workflows buy repeatability but become rigid and fragile: they struggle with unexpected inputs because the path is fixed, errors compound across steps, every handoff needs a quality check, and changing one step can silently break downstream steps. In RAG these show up as weak retrieval (the right chunk isn't found), bad chunking (context split or lost), noisy context (irrelevant passages distract the model), and compounding errors where an early retrieval mistake corrupts later turns. Because a fixed pipeline can't self-correct, you mitigate with validation gates at each handoff, evaluation/monitoring, better chunking and reranking, and - when brittleness dominates - moving toward more adaptive agentic designs.

interview.question: What is the difference between an AI workflow and an AI agent, and when do you choose each?
interview.model_answer: A workflow is a fixed orchestration: the developer hardcodes the control flow, so the same predefined steps run every time - Input through Task 1..n to Output. An agent uses model-directed control flow: the LLM plans, picks the next action, calls tools, observes results, and loops until the goal is met, so the sequence of steps is decided at run time. The crisp distinction is who owns the control flow - the developer (workflow) or the model (agent). Choose a workflow for well-defined tasks that need predictability and consistency; choose an agent for open-ended problems where you can't predict the number of steps or hardcode a fixed path, like a coding agent or a web-browsing agent. Prefer the workflow when it's sufficient, since agents cost more determinism, latency, and debuggability.

agent = model-directed control flow: plan -> act (tools) -> observe -> loop

workflow for predictable/well-defined tasks; agent for open-ended problems
agent examples: coding agent, web-browsing agent

interview.question: Explain the ReAct framework. What problem does it solve and what is the loop?
interview.model_answer: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves Reasoning and Acting in one framework instead of treating chain-of-thought reasoning and action generation as separate abilities. The motivation is that reasoning alone hallucinates and propagates errors because it isn't grounded, while acting alone lacks high-level planning and can't reason over its results. Interleaving them creates a synergy: reasoning decides the next action, and the action's observation feeds back to update the reasoning. Mechanically the model loops over Thought -> Action -> Observation, e.g. Thought: I should look this up; Act: Search[...]; Obs: the returned text; repeat until Act: Finish[answer]. This plan-act-observe loop is the backbone of modern tool-using agents.
key_points: ReAct = Reasoning + Acting, interleaved in a unified framework
Yao et al., Princeton & Google, 2022
reasoning alone: hallucination + error propagation (no grounding)
acting alone: lacks planning / reasoning over results

foundation of modern tool-using agents

interview.question: What's the difference between chain-of-thought prompting and a reasoning model, and what is test-time compute?
interview.model_answer: Chain-of-thought is a prompting technique that coaxes a standard model into producing intermediate steps, giving some reasoning ability - it 'can write a scratch pad.' A reasoning model has its reasoning baked in during training and architecture design, so it 'can actually use the scratch pad to work out the answer.' Reasoning models are trained on data rich in human reasoning traces, learn patterns of math, coding, logic, and problem-solving, and are refined with reinforcement learning that rewards correct solutions to hard problems. Test-time compute is the lever of spending more inference compute to 'think longer' before answering, which improves hard-problem accuracy - a scaling axis distinct from training-time scaling.

reasoning model = reasoning optimized in training + architecture

interview.question: What kinds of reasoning do reasoning models show, and how is that different from what an AI agent does?
interview.model_answer: Reasoning models exhibit behaviors like decomposing a problem ('let's do it step by step'), self-reflection ('wait, let me reconsider'), and verification ('let me double-check'). These are internal capabilities of the model - they happen within the model's own generated reasoning tokens. AI-agent execution is different: the agent takes external actions in an orchestration loop, like calling tools, retrieving documents, running code, and observing real results. So a reasoning model can self-decompose and self-verify without touching the outside world, while an agent grounds its steps in actual tool feedback. Good systems combine both: a reasoning model as the brain inside an agent's act-observe loop.

interview.question: Walk through how function calling / tool use works between an LLM and an application.
interview.model_answer: Function calling wraps external APIs - a calculator, calendar, search, a weather API - as tools with a name and typed parameters, and the model decides when to use them from the prompt and its planning. The loop: (1) the developer passes the tool definitions plus the user request to the model; (2) the model decides a tool is needed and returns a structured tool call - crucially it does not execute anything; (3) the application executes the function and gets structured data back, e.g. get_weather('paris') -> {'temperature': 14}; (4) the developer sends that result back to the model as context along with prior messages; (5) the model turns the result into the final answer like 'It's currently 14C in Paris.' The separation - model requests, application executes, result returned as context - is what grounds the answer and keeps execution controlled, and it's the mechanism under ReAct-style agents.

interview.question: What are the major components of an AI agent?
interview.model_answer: An agent has four major parts. First, the LLM reasoning loop - the brain that plans, decides the next action, and processes observations, looping until the task is done. Second, tools - the ways it acts on the world: APIs, MCP servers, search, files, databases. Third, context management - handling the working context, like chat history and context compression, to stay within the window. Fourth, memory - persistent storage of preferences and task state across steps or sessions. Structurally it's an Input -> Planning <-> Tools -> Output loop where planning and tool use cycle. Together these give the agent model-driven control flow (reasoning loop), grounding and action (tools), and coherence over many steps (context + memory), which is what distinguishes it from a fixed workflow.

interview.question: What are the minimal building blocks to code a simple AI agent, and what are some real examples?
interview.model_answer: A minimal agent is three things: a reasoning model as the brain that plans, a set of function calls / tools it can invoke, and an agent loop that repeats plan -> act -> observe until the task is done. That recipe covers small projects like a travel assistant (check weather, book tickets, suggest options), a calendar assistant (schedule and resolve conflicts), a research agent (gather sources and write a brief), or a shopping agent (compare products to a request). interview.question: Walk me through the core agent loop. Who actually runs the tools, and what stops the loop?
interview.model_answer: You maintain a running message list seeded with the system prompt and the user message. Each turn you call the LLM with the messages plus the tool schemas. The model returns either tool calls or a final text answer. If it returns tool calls, the *runtime* (your code) executes each function, appends the results back into the messages, and loops so the model can see the results and continue reasoning. If it returns no tool calls, that's the final answer and you break. Because the LLM is stateless you re-send the whole history each turn. The loop is bounded by a `max_iterations` cap (and usually a token/cost budget) so a confused model can't spin forever. The agent is essentially a controlled runtime wrapped around the model.
key_points: agent = controlled runtime around a stateless model
loop: input -> plan -> tool call -> execute -> feed result back -> repeat -> output

interview.question: What exactly is 'context' for an LLM agent, and why does it matter that output tokens become input tokens?
interview.model_answer: Context is everything the model can see for the current task - its whiteboard. On the input side that's the system prompt, the tool schemas, the chat history, any retrieved documents, and the current user request. On the output side it's the model's reasoning, its text response, and its tool calls. The key dynamic in an agent is that each turn's output (the assistant message and tool results) gets appended and re-sent as input on the next turn, so the context strictly grows across a session. Since the window is finite and every token adds cost and latency, managing what occupies context is the central engineering problem. You inspect it with tracing tools like LangSmith or, in Claude Code, the `/context` command.

interview.question: Why does an agent's context window fill up over a long run, and what breaks when it does?
interview.model_answer: Because the model is stateless, every turn re-sends the full trajectory and appends the new turn on top - the user's messages, the model's reasoning, its tool calls, and every tool result. Nothing is removed automatically, so the token count grows monotonically. Three things break as it grows: cost and latency climb linearly with input size; important early information gets buried under noise and 'lost in the middle'; and eventually you hit the context-window ceiling and the request fails or must be truncated. That is the motivation for context engineering - deciding what to keep, what to summarize (compaction), what to move out of the prompt (offloading), and what to isolate to a subagent.
