interview.question: Define context engineering. Given a symptom, which technique do you reach for?
interview.model_answer: Context engineering is the discipline of putting just the right information in the context window at each step - not the most information. The mantra is 'if everything is important, nothing is important': padding the window dilutes the signal and hurts both quality and cost. I map symptoms to tools: if the agent needs consistent rules and behavior, that goes in the system prompt; if it needs external knowledge or to take actions, that's function calling or MCP; if the conversation history has grown noisy, that's compaction; if there are too many tools or the task is too complex for one context, that's subagents / context isolation; and if it needs to remember across sessions, that's memory. They compose - a real agent uses several at once.
key_points: goal: the right information at each step, not the most
'if everything is important, nothing is important'
system prompt -> consistent behavior/rules
function calling / MCP -> external knowledge and actions
compaction -> history growth; subagents -> too many tools/complex tasks; memory -> cross-session
common_mistakes: Equating more context with better answers
Stuffing everything into the system prompt
Treating the practices as mutually exclusive
followups: Give an example where adding more context made an agent worse.
How do you decide between compaction and offloading for a long run?

interview.question: What belongs in a system prompt versus a user message versus a tool? Sketch a good system prompt.
interview.model_answer: The system prompt should define behavior, not perform the task. It carries the durable, cross-request stuff: the assistant's Role, its Job (what success looks like), its Priorities (what to optimize for), and its Boundaries (what not to do). Task-specific details - this particular request, its inputs - belong in the user messages, because they change every call. Reusable step-by-step procedures belong in tools or skills. So a travel assistant's system prompt states the date and role, tells it to use tools proactively and only when relevant, and to ask for clarification when the destination or dates are missing - but the actual trip request comes in as a user message. In Claude Code this pattern shows up as CLAUDE.md, the project instructions created with /init that steer behavior for a repo. Keeping the system prompt stable also makes it cacheable.
key_points: system prompt defines behavior, doesn't do the whole job
contains Role, Job, Priorities, Boundaries
policy -> system prompt; task details -> user messages; procedures -> tools/skills
Claude Code: CLAUDE.md (via /init) supplies project instructions
keep it stable so it stays cache-friendly
common_mistakes: Putting per-request task details in the system prompt
Writing a system prompt that tries to do the task instead of setting behavior
Interpolating volatile values (live timestamps, IDs) that break prompt caching
followups: How would you A/B test two system prompts for the same agent?
Why can putting a live timestamp in the system prompt hurt your cache hit rate?

interview.question: A teammate says the model 'runs the function' and that better tool selection just needs a smarter model. Correct both.
interview.model_answer: The model does not run the function. In a tool call the model does four things: picks a tool, produces structured arguments matching the schema, waits, and then continues reasoning once the result comes back. The actual execution is done by the runtime - your code or a server-side tool - which returns the result into the context. Second, tool selection is not mostly raw intelligence; it's heavily shaped by how the tools are defined. Give each tool a narrow purpose, clear self-describing parameter names, and no ambiguous overlap with sibling tools, and describe *when* to call it, not just what it does. Vague descriptions and overlapping tools produce wrong or missed calls even from a strong model. So tool definitions are prompt engineering - iterate on them, not just on the model.
key_points: function calls are where answering becomes acting
model: choose tool -> structured args -> wait -> continue reasoning
the runtime executes the function, not the model
good tools: narrow purpose, clear param names, no ambiguous overlap
tool choice is shaped by the definition, not just model intelligence
common_mistakes: Believing the model executes the tool itself
Blaming the model for wrong tool calls when the schemas overlap or are vague
Writing tool descriptions that say what it does but never when to use it
followups: How would you redesign two overlapping tools the model keeps confusing?
Where do you gate a destructive tool call (e.g. send_email) for human approval?

interview.question: What problem does MCP solve, and why is calling it 'just another function-calling format' wrong?
interview.model_answer: MCP - the Model Context Protocol, proposed by Anthropic and now adopted broadly - standardizes how agents connect to external tools, data, and reusable workflows across different systems. Before MCP you wrote a bespoke integration for every agent-to-service pair; MCP makes it one protocol, so any MCP-speaking client can discover and use any MCP server (file system, Git, project management, time, and so on). Calling it 'just another function-calling format' undersells it: it isn't only about invoking a function, it's about discoverable context - the server advertises the tools and resources it exposes, and the agent routes calls to it when the model decides it needs them, then folds the result into the answer. It's an interoperability protocol, and it's related to but distinct from skills, which package procedures rather than provide a connection standard.
key_points: MCP standardizes agent connections to external tools, data, and workflows
proposed by Anthropic, adopted widely (OpenAI, etc.)
a broader interoperability protocol, not just a function-calling format
about discoverable context: servers advertise tools and resources
example servers: file system, Git, task management, time
common_mistakes: Describing MCP as merely a new JSON tool-call shape
Confusing MCP (connection protocol) with skills (packaged procedures)
Assuming every agent needs a custom integration per external service
followups: How does an MCP client discover what a server exposes?
When would you build a custom function tool instead of using an MCP server?

interview.question: Why is RAG a context-engineering tool, and how do you choose among keyword, embedding, and graph retrieval?
interview.model_answer: RAG is how you decide what external information enters the context window - it's the gate on what the model gets to see for this request, so it's squarely a context-engineering tool, and in an agent it's typically exposed as a retrieval function the model can call. It's not a single method but a family, and you choose by query shape. Exact strings - IDs, function names, error messages - are best served by keyword/grep search: fast, cheap, precise. When the wording varies but the meaning is the same, like a paraphrased natural-language question, embedding/semantic retrieval wins. When relationships and multi-hop connections matter - dependency chains, org structure, linked entities - a knowledge graph is the right tool. In practice I often combine them and let the agent pick, and I rerank/compress the results so retrieval doesn't blow up the context.
key_points: RAG decides what external info enters the context window
usually implemented as a retrieval function call in an agent
keyword/grep: exact strings, IDs, error messages - fast/cheap/precise
embedding/semantic: paraphrases, natural-language questions
knowledge graph: relationships, dependency chains, multi-hop facts
common_mistakes: Treating embeddings as the only retrieval method
Using semantic search for exact IDs where grep is more precise
Injecting all retrieved text without reranking or compression
followups: How would you build a hybrid retriever and let the agent choose the method?
What signals tell you your embedding retrieval is returning off-topic chunks?

interview.question: RAG is blowing up your context window. Walk through a 'retrieve more, keep less' pipeline.
interview.model_answer: Naive RAG concatenates every retrieved chunk, so context grows fast and quality drops. The pattern is retrieve more, keep less. First rewrite the user request together with the current task state into a sharper query. Then retrieve a broad candidate set - say top-k of 12 - to get high recall. Then rerank and keep only the best handful, maybe the top 4, for precision. Finally compress each survivor with a summarizer down to a small token budget, around 120 tokens each, so only the signal reaches the model. The window stays small even though you searched broadly. The natural follow-up is: what if you need the raw documents later? You keep the compressed summaries in-prompt and offload the full docs to files or a store, fetching them on demand rather than carrying them.
key_points: retrieve more, keep less: wide recall then aggressive narrowing
rewrite the query using user request + task state
retrieve broad (top_k), then rerank down to a few
compress/summarize each survivor to a small token budget
keep raw docs available via offloading, fetch on demand
common_mistakes: Dumping all top_k chunks straight into the prompt
Skipping rerank, so low-precision hits waste context
Discarding the raw documents instead of offloading them for later
followups: How do you tune top_k and the rerank cutoff for a given latency budget?
How does summarizing chunks risk losing information you needed?

interview.question: What is context compaction, when do you trigger it, and what must a good compaction preserve?
interview.model_answer: Compaction distills a long, noisy agent history into a concise state so the agent stays focused and you cut token cost and latency. You trigger it when the window is filling up - long message history, raw tool logs, full file dumps, retrieved docs - typically at a token threshold. The transformation replaces the full history with a compressed task state - the key decisions made, the active constraints, and the next step - plus distilled evidence like a log summary and the source references that matter (the specific files touched). The rule is that good compaction shortens details but preserves important facts: keep decisions, open questions, constraints, and artifacts; drop brainstorming, dead ends, repeated clarifications, and raw 500-line log dumps. What you must not lose is anything that changes what the agent does next.
key_points: compaction distills prior context into a concise state
trigger when history/tool-output/docs make the window noisy or full
keep decisions, open questions, constraints, artifacts
drop brainstorming, dead ends, raw log/file dumps
shorten details but preserve important facts
common_mistakes: Summarizing so aggressively that a load-bearing constraint is lost
Compacting away the artifacts/source references the agent still needs
Never compacting, so cost and 'lost in the middle' degrade quality
followups: How is compaction different from context offloading?
How do you validate that a compaction didn't drop something the agent needed?

interview.question: Explain context offloading with the backpack-and-map metaphor, and how it differs from compaction.
interview.model_answer: The metaphor is: don't make the model carry the warehouse - give it a backpack and a map. You keep only the minimum useful working set in the prompt, move big state out of the prompt, and fetch it on demand through retrieval, files, tools, or memory. The Manus example shows it: instead of leaving a giant observation - the full contents of a document or file - inline in context where it inflates every later turn, you write it to the file system and keep just a reference; the agent re-reads the file only when it needs the content again. The difference from compaction is what happens to the data: compaction summarizes what stays in the window, so detail is lost by design; offloading moves the full state out and leaves a pointer, so nothing is lost and the raw data is retrievable. That's why offloading answers 'what if I need the raw documents later?' - the summary can't, the offloaded file can.
key_points: keep the minimum working set in the prompt
move big state outside; fetch on demand
fetch via retrieval, files, tools, or memory
Manus example: write large observations to the file system, keep a reference
offloading preserves raw data (pointer); compaction summarizes (lossy)
common_mistakes: Leaving large tool observations inline in every turn
Confusing offloading with compaction (moving vs summarizing)
Offloading without giving the agent a reliable way to fetch it back
followups: When would you offload to files vs to a vector store vs to memory?
What are the failure modes if the agent can't reliably re-fetch offloaded state?

interview.question: How do subagents implement context isolation, and what does the main agent get back?
interview.model_answer: Context isolation means each agent only sees the slice of context relevant to its job. Rather than passing one universal conversation transcript to every agent and tool, you partition context and tools by role - a transportation context with flight/train/car tools, a hotel context, a dining context. When the main agent needs a sub-task done, it delegates with isolated context: it sends the subagent only what's needed - the task, dates, budget, preferences - not the full history. The subagent runs in its own limited context window with just task-specific input and the relevant tools, and returns a summarized result, like the top 3 flights with prices, rather than its entire working trace. The main agent integrates that summary and continues. The benefits are concrete: less noise and interference, each agent stays within its window limits, and you get better accuracy, privacy, and efficiency because the subagent never sees unrelated data.
key_points: context isolation keeps each agent focused on only what it needs
partition context/tools by role instead of one universal transcript
main agent delegates with isolated context (only task-relevant inputs)
subagent runs in its own window and returns a summarized result
benefits: less noise/interference, window limits, accuracy, privacy, efficiency
common_mistakes: Passing the full conversation transcript to every subagent and tool
Returning the subagent's entire trace instead of a summary
Over-splitting into subagents for work a single context handles fine
followups: When is a subagent overkill versus just calling a tool?
How does spawning a subagent interact with prompt caching on the main loop?

interview.question: How does prompt caching work, and why is 'always keep the context stable to get cache hits' wrong?
interview.model_answer: Prompt caching lets the provider reuse a large, stable prefix instead of reprocessing it, cutting cost and latency on repeat requests. It works by prefix match: everything from the start of the prompt up to the first differing byte is reused, so cache-friendly design puts stable content first - a frozen system prompt, a deterministic tool list - and only appends new content at the end. Editing something in the middle invalidates the whole cache after that point, so across agent steps you want to append the latest action and observation, not rewrite earlier turns. But the misconception is treating cache stability as a quality goal. It's purely a cost/latency optimization. You should not preserve bad or stale context just to win a cache hit - if compacting or correcting the context improves the answer, do it; the quality gain beats the cache saving. I'd also verify hits, for example via cache_read_input_tokens, since a live timestamp in the prefix silently kills caching.
key_points: stable prefixes are cached to cut cost and latency
caching is a prefix match - reuse up to the first differing byte
cache-friendly design: stable content first, append new content last
cache stability is an optimization, not a quality goal
don't preserve bad context just to get a cache hit
common_mistakes: Keeping stale/bad context frozen just to preserve a cache hit
Interpolating volatile values (timestamps, IDs) into the prefix and silently breaking caching
Rewriting earlier turns instead of appending, invalidating the cache
followups: How would you diagnose a cache hit rate that dropped to zero?
How do compaction and prompt caching trade off against each other?

interview.question: Agents are built on stateless LLMs. Distinguish the context window from memory, and explain why cross-session memory is needed.
interview.model_answer: The LLM itself is stateless - the context window is the only thing it 'sees'. Within a session, the agent loop appends each turn and re-sends the whole window, so the model appears to remember - but that memory is just the growing context. Start a new session and the window resets to zero, so the agent forgets everything: tell it in session 1 that you like Thai food, then say 'order some food for me' in session 2, and it has no idea what kind. Cross-session memory closes that gap by persisting useful facts outside the window and reloading them into future sessions. ChatGPT memory does this for durable user preferences with a management UI; Claude Code's auto memory selectively saves things like code styles, build commands, and conventions - for instance remembering 'use uv, not pip' - into per-project files under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/, editable with /memory. The design decisions are what to save, when to write it, and how to load it into the next session's context.
key_points: LLMs are stateless; the context window is all the model sees
in-session 'memory' is just the growing, re-sent context window
new session -> fresh window -> the agent forgets prior sessions
memory persists facts outside the window and reloads them later
examples: ChatGPT memory; Claude Code auto memory (/memory, per-project files)
common_mistakes: Conflating the context window with true persistent memory
Assuming an agent remembers a prior session automatically
Saving everything to memory instead of selective, useful facts
followups: What should and shouldn't be written to memory, and how do you avoid storing secrets?
When is memory triggered to write, and how is it loaded into the next session?

interview.question: What is 'harness engineering', and why doesn't a stronger model make it unnecessary?
interview.model_answer: Harness engineering is building the software that surrounds the LLM — the environment it acts in, the feedback loops that tell it what happened, and the control systems that constrain it — so the overall agent is reliable. The core practice (per Hashimoto) is: every time the agent makes a mistake, engineer a permanent fix so it never repeats it, so reliability compounds over time. It is not a single ideal design; it's choosing the right surrounding components for a specific model and task. A stronger model does not remove the need — because a more capable, more autonomous model can take bigger, riskier actions, so it needs *better* control, validation and guardrails, not fewer. The model can, however, make some individual components obsolete (e.g. hand-written scaffolding it no longer needs).
key_points: harness = environments + feedback loops + control systems around the LLM
Hashimoto: engineer a permanent fix so the mistake never recurs; fixes compound
not one ideal design — select the right components for the model+task
stronger models make the harness MORE important (more autonomy -> more control/validation)
but a stronger model can retire some individual harness components
common_mistakes: Equating agent quality with model quality and ignoring the surrounding system
Believing there is a single universal 'best' harness
Treating fixes as one-off patches instead of permanent, compounding improvements
followups: Give an example of a harness fix that stops a specific class of agent mistake.

interview.question: What are the main components of an agent harness, and why enumerate them?
interview.model_answer: A harness decomposes into: the system prompt, tools (function calling / MCP), context compaction, subagents, memory, the runtime (loop + environment + policy), skills, and evaluation. Enumerating them turns the vague goal 'make the agent more reliable' into targeted engineering: when the agent fails you localize it to a layer — a bad tool schema, missing or stale memory, context overflow that compaction should have handled, a runtime that couldn't enforce a policy, or a missing eval that let a regression through — and fix that layer. Good reference implementations to learn the patterns from are Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.
key_points: components: system prompt, tools/MCP, compaction, subagents, memory, runtime, skills, eval
each layer is a separate place to diagnose and fix failures
reference implementations: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode
harness engineering = tuning these surrounding components, not the weights
common_mistakes: Treating the agent as a monolith so every failure looks like 'the model is bad'
Skipping evaluation as a first-class harness component
followups: Where does MCP fit in the harness and what does it standardize?
Which component would you add first for a brand-new agent and why?

interview.question: Someone says 'my agent runtime is just the model in a while-loop.' What's missing, and why does the distinction matter?
interview.model_answer: A real runtime is Policy + Environment + Loop, not just the loop. The Loop is the control flow deciding the next step; the Environment is the execution surface the agent actually acts on (filesystem, shell, browser, container, APIs, network); the Policy is the rules constraining what it may do (permissions, egress limits, approval gates). The distinction matters because of one principle: the prompt can *state* policy but only the runtime can *enforce* it. If safety lives only in the system prompt, a single jailbreak, hallucination, or unexpected tool output bypasses it. Putting policy in the environment — a sandbox that physically can't reach production, a tool wrapper that checks permissions before executing — makes the constraint real regardless of what the model decides to do.
key_points: Runtime = Policy + Environment + Loop
Loop = control flow; Environment = execution surface; Policy = constraints
the prompt STATES policy; only the runtime ENFORCES it
'the model is not your runtime — the loop is'
simplest runtime is an observe/think/act Python loop with a budget guard
common_mistakes: Putting safety only in the system prompt and calling it a control
Conflating the model with the runtime
Ignoring the environment and policy layers entirely
followups: Give a concrete policy that a prompt cannot enforce but the runtime can.
How does the budget/turn guard in the loop prevent runaway agents?

interview.question: Why might exposing a shell/CLI to an agent beat a curated set of function-calling tools?
interview.model_answer: Two reasons. First, a unified language: the CLI lets the agent plan and execute in the same vocabulary, instead of translating intent into a small fixed set of bespoke tools. Second and biggest, composability belongs in the runtime — shell primitives combine via pipes (`|`), sequencing (`&&`, `||`, `;`) and redirection (`>`, `2>&1`), so a handful of commands compose into a huge behavior space. `cat app.log | grep ERROR | wc -l` needs no dedicated 'count errors' tool. That keeps the tool surface small while capability stays broad. The trade-off is safety: a shell is powerful, so it must run inside a sandbox with policy (this is exactly why the runtime's real boundary is the sandbox, not the prompt).
key_points: CLI gives a unified language for planning AND execution
composability is the CLI's biggest runtime advantage — put composition in the runtime
pipes | , sequencing && || ; , redirection > >> 2>&1
few primitives + operators = large behavior space; avoids tool-per-combination sprawl
power demands a sandbox + policy around the shell
common_mistakes: Adding a new bespoke tool for every task combination instead of composing primitives
Exposing a raw shell with no sandbox or policy
Assuming narrow typed tools are always safer/better than a CLI
followups: What are the downsides of giving an agent a full shell, and how do you mitigate them?

interview.question: Where is an agent's real safety boundary, and what exactly should a sandbox control?
interview.model_answer: The real safety boundary is the sandbox, not the system prompt. A prompt only *states* policy; the sandbox *enforces* it by controlling the four things that determine blast radius: which files the agent can read/write, which processes it can spawn, which network destinations it can reach, and which secrets/credentials are even visible to it. The point is to let the agent act freely inside pre-defined limits — a real workspace for intermediate files and safe network access — while guaranteeing that even a jailbroken or hallucinating model can't exfiltrate secrets or touch production, because those capabilities aren't in the sandbox at all. Real examples: Claude Code's sandboxed bash and cloud sandboxes, OpenAI's Responses API shell tool with a hosted container, and OpenClaw's gateway runtime with explicit permissions.
key_points: the sandbox is the runtime's real guardrail, not the prompt
controls files, processes, network egress, and visible secrets/credentials
'act freely inside pre-defined limits' — freedom bounded by the sandbox
contains blast radius even when the model misbehaves
examples: Claude Code sandboxed bash, OpenAI Responses shell+container, OpenClaw gateway
common_mistakes: Relying on prompt instructions ('do not access X') as a security control
Leaving real credentials/network reachable inside the agent's environment
Confusing capability restriction with just filtering the model's outputs

interview.question: How do 'help' output and error messages function as parts of an agent's runtime, and how should you design them?
interview.model_answer: Both are control-loop primitives, not cosmetics. 'Help' should support progressive discovery: rather than pre-loading long manuals into context (which wastes tokens and dilutes attention), let the agent run `--help` on demand and pull in exactly the reference it needs when it needs it. Error messages steer the very next action, so a good error says three things: what failed, why it likely failed, and what to try next. 'Error: invalid input' gives the agent nothing to act on; 'Cannot open photo.png with cat because it is a binary image; use `see photo.png` or `metadata photo.png`' names the cause and hands over a concrete recovery path, turning a failure into a self-correcting step. Designing rich, actionable errors is one of the highest-leverage harness fixes because it prevents whole classes of retry loops.
key_points: help = progressive discovery; don't stuff long docs into context
error messages are part of the control loop; they steer the next action
good error = what failed + why + what to try next
'invalid input' is useless; name the cause and suggest the recovery command
actionable errors prevent retry/thrashing loops (a high-leverage harness fix)
common_mistakes: Pre-loading entire tool manuals into the system prompt
Returning opaque errors like 'invalid input' or a raw stack trace with no guidance
Not suggesting a next action the agent can actually take
followups: How does progressive discovery relate to context-window budgeting?

interview.question: When would you implement a process as a coded workflow versus an agent Skill?
interview.model_answer: Use a coded workflow when the process is stable and must run identically every time: code is deterministic, the control flow is exact, and branches are enforced by the system — ideal for compliance-critical or high-frequency paths. Use a Skill when inputs are messy or judgment is needed: a Skill is an instruction-level workflow whose branches are *suggested* to the model, not guaranteed, so it flexes when the situation needs interpretation, adaptation, or explanation. Crucially a Skill is a *soft* workflow — reusable knowledge that helps the model decide better — it is not a determinism mechanism. It is also not 'just a saved prompt' or mere documentation; it packages procedures and playbooks around the capabilities that tools/MCP provide. If you truly need a guaranteed branch (e.g. always ask before overwrite), enforce it in code, not in a Skill.
key_points: workflow-in-code: deterministic, exact control flow, system-enforced branches
skill: instruction-level, branches suggested not guaranteed, flexible under messy inputs
skill = soft workflow + reusable knowledge that improves decisions
skills wrap procedures/playbooks around tool/MCP capabilities
misconceptions: skill != determinism, != saved prompt, != documentation
common_mistakes: Expecting a Skill to guarantee a branch/step every run (that needs code)
Dismissing a Skill as just a prompt or a doc file
Hard-coding a rigid workflow where messy inputs actually need judgment

interview.question: How is a Skill structured on disk, and how does progressive loading keep it from bloating the context window?
interview.model_answer: A Skill is a directory whose entry point is `SKILL.md`: YAML frontmatter with a `name` and a concise `description`, followed by Markdown instructions. Anything heavy is bundled as sibling files the SKILL.md links to — `reference.md`, a `forms.md` sub-procedure, and runnable scripts like `extract_fields.py`. Progressive disclosure means only each skill's short name+description is loaded up front (appended to the system prompt as a lightweight catalog). The model selects the relevant skill from that catalog, and only *then* are the full instructions loaded — in a coding agent that's literally the model running `cat skills/pdf/SKILL.md`, and following a reference to `cat skills/pdf/forms.md` only if needed. So the context holds N cheap descriptions instead of N full skill bodies, and the expensive detail is paid for only on the one skill actually used, one hop at a time.
key_points: SKILL.md = YAML frontmatter (name, description) + Markdown instructions
bundle extras as sibling files: reference.md, forms.md, scripts (extract_fields.py)
up front, only short name+description of each skill enters context (a catalog)
select relevant skill first, then load its heavy instructions on demand
loading is file reads: cat SKILL.md, then follow references to forms.md/reference.md
common_mistakes: Loading every skill's full instructions into the system prompt at all times

interview.question: Concretely, how does a Skill get added to an agent and how does the agent access it at runtime?
interview.model_answer: On the configuration side an agent has a core system prompt, a set of equipped Skills, and equipped MCP servers (possibly proxying remote MCP servers). On the computer side the agent has a VM with Bash/Python/Node and a filesystem — and the actual *contents* of each skill directory live in that filesystem, e.g. `skills/pdf/` holding SKILL.md, forms.md, reference.md and extract_fields.py. So equipping a skill is essentially placing its directory on the agent's computer. At runtime the agent 'uses the computer': it reads SKILL.md with bash (`cat`), follows references to other files, and executes bundled scripts with python. Because a skill is just files plus scripts, it composes cleanly with the CLI environment and is contained by the same sandbox — no special skill runtime is needed.

agent VM: Bash/Python/Node + a filesystem holding the skill directories

equipping a skill = dropping its directory into the agent's filesystem

interview.question: Why can't you 'add evals later', and why is evaluating an agent harder than evaluating a single LLM response?
interview.model_answer: Skipping evals early puts you in a reactive loop: prod breaks, you patch it, the patch shifts behavior elsewhere, a new failure appears — with no eval you can't even see the regressions your patches cause. Evals catch behavior changes before users do, and their value compounds: every check keeps guarding the system as the agent evolves, so you want the baseline in place before, not after, the agent 'works'. Agent eval is harder because an agent isn't a single string to grade — it's a multi-turn system that calls tools, mutates files/DBs, adapts to intermediate results, and compounds errors across steps. So instead of `grade(response_text)` you grade the full transcript, the outcome (final environment state), the tool_use/actions, and even the memory_effect on the next session. That's four surfaces of correctness instead of one.
key_points: no evals -> reactive patch cycle where fixes cause new regressions
evals surface regressions early; their protective value compounds over time
misconception: 'add evals later after it works' (you lose the baseline)
agents are multi-turn: tools, file/DB mutations, adaptation, compounding errors
grade transcript + outcome + tool_use + memory_effect, not just response_text
common_mistakes: Deferring evaluation until after launch

interview.question: Define Task, Run, Transcript, and Outcome for agent evaluation, and list the dimensions you'd actually score.
interview.model_answer: A Task is the test case: an input plus explicit success criteria. A Run (or Trial) is one attempt at that Task. The Transcript/trace is everything that happened during the run — messages, tool calls, planning steps, outputs. The Outcome is the final environment state: files written, DB rows changed, tests passing, bookings made. Given those, you score several dimensions, not just correctness: (1) outcome correctness — did it truly succeed; (2) trace quality — were the steps and tool choices good; (3) safety/policy — did it avoid risky behavior; (4) efficiency — turns, retries, tokens, seconds; (5) quality — for open-ended work, how good the result is. Structurally this is an eval suite of Tasks, each carrying its graders and tracked metrics, each run for multiple trials, and a grader maps trajectory+outcome to scores. Scoring only outcome misses an agent that got the right answer via unsafe or wasteful steps.

interview.question: What is agent instrumentation, how do you add it, and why isn't it 'just logging'?
interview.model_answer: Instrumentation is the structured capture of what an agent did — the full trace, every tool call and its arguments, outputs and errors, plus latency, retries and token usage. It's the raw material without which you can't evaluate, read transcripts, or debug. You add it with tracing: wrap major steps (planner, tool call, retriever, validator, final response) in spans/events so a run becomes a timed, causally-linked tree, typically emitted via OpenTelemetry and stored in a tool like Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust, or Arize Phoenix. It isn't 'just logging' because logs are flat, unstructured lines; instrumentation produces linked spans carrying arguments, timings, and token/retry counts that you can aggregate, filter, replay and attach grades to. interview.question: What are the three types of evaluation graders, and how do you decide which to use?
interview.model_answer: Deterministic graders — unit tests, assertions, schema checks, exact state validation — are best for correctness, safety gates, and reproducible scoring: they're fast, cheap, and variance-free. Model-based graders (LLM-as-judge) do rubric scoring, pairwise comparison, and trace-quality judging, which is useful for open-ended quality where exact checks are too rigid, at the cost of some noise and needing their own validation. Human graders give expert review for ambiguous, subjective, or high-stakes cases where nuance beats automation, but they don't scale. The decision rule is a ladder: deterministic when you can, model when you must, humans when it matters most — pick the cheapest, most reproducible grader that can genuinely judge the property, and escalate only when it can't. A single task usually carries several graders together (a deterministic test plus an LLM rubric plus a state check plus a tool-call check).

human: expert review for ambiguous / subjective / high-stakes cases

interview.question: Aggregate eval scores dropped but you don't know why. How do you use transcripts to diagnose it?
interview.model_answer: Scores say *that* it regressed; transcripts say *why*. First confirm it's a real failure, not a grader failure — the agent may have succeeded in a way the grader misjudged. Then read failed runs and compare them against successful ones to isolate the difference. Find the *first* point the agent went off track, not merely where it finally errored, and at that step check whether it had the right context, the right tool, and useful feedback — and whether the error messages and validation signals actually helped it recover. Watch for loops, retries, and tool thrashing as signatures of a harness problem. Attribute each failure to the model, the harness, the tools, or the environment. Finally, group similar failures so they become durable harness fixes (a missing tool, a clearer error) rather than one-off patches — that's how transcript reading feeds back into harness engineering.

interview.question: Contrast offline and online evaluation for an agent, and describe how you'd sequence them.
interview.model_answer: Offline evaluation runs on static datasets with controlled metrics: reproducible, cheap, and safe, so it's ideal for gating changes and catching regressions before release — but it can't observe real traffic, real users, or full-system effects. Online evaluation runs against the real dataset and adds user-facing metrics like satisfaction and conversion, and it evaluates the whole system including scale, latency, and integrations. Its typical methods are A/B tests (split live traffic between variants) and shadow deployments (run the new agent alongside production on real inputs without affecting users). The sequence is 'start offline, graduate online, then iterate': validate cheaply offline, promote a candidate to a shadow or A/B online test to measure true user and system impact, then fold what you learn back into the offline suite and repeat.

interview.question: What is a self-evolving agent, what exactly does it 'improve' if it isn't retraining weights, and how does Hermes implement this?
interview.model_answer: A self-evolving agent autonomously diagnoses its own failures and rewrites its own logic to permanently improve — the step from an agent that *executes* code to one that *rewrites* code. Since it isn't touching model weights, what it optimizes is its configuration: system prompts, tool JSON descriptions, routing logic, and explicitly defined skills — its config files become a search space an optimizer navigates. Concretely that's load the prompt file, have an optimizer rewrite it from feedback, save it back — not inventing new languages or doing gradient updates. Hermes is a reference implementation: (1) agent-curated memory — on a timed internal nudge with no user input, it evaluates recent turns and, if worth keeping, writes to a MEMORY.md that persists across sessions; (2) autonomous skill creation — on task completion it decides if the path is worth documenting based on triggers (5+ tool calls, recovery from an error, a user correction, or a successful non-obvious workflow) and writes a reusable skill file to ~/.hermes/skills/; (3) skill self-improvement via a skill_manage tool with six actions (create, patch, edit, delete, write_file, remove_file), preferring `patch` for targeted, token-efficient edits over a full `edit` rewrite that could break working code.

interview.question: Why does an LLM have to generate text one token at a time instead of producing the whole output at once?
interview.model_answer: An LLM predicts the next token from a probability distribution conditioned on all the tokens seen so far. Because each new token depends on the entire preceding sequence, the model cannot compute a later token until the earlier ones have actually been chosen and appended. So generation is inherently sequential: sample a token, feed it back in as part of the context, and repeat the loop. This is what 'autoregressive' means, and it's why latency scales with the number of tokens you generate rather than being a single one-shot computation.

interview.question: How does a fixed vocabulary of tens of thousands of sub-word tokens still cover typos and rare words?
interview.model_answer: The key idea is compositionality: instead of needing one entry per word, the tokenizer breaks any string down into smaller sub-word pieces it does know. That means there are effectively no true out-of-vocabulary words, since anything can be spelled out from the pieces in the vocabulary. interview.question: In a decoder, what behavior does a causal mask enforce?
interview.model_answer: A causal mask forces each decoder position to attend only to itself and earlier tokens, blocking any attention to future positions. Concretely, it sets the attention scores for future positions to negative infinity before the softmax, so those weights become zero. This preserves the autoregressive property: when predicting the next token, the model can't peek at tokens it hasn't generated yet, which is essential for consistency between training and inference. Without it, the model would leak future information during teacher-forced training and fail to generate left-to-right at inference.

interview.question: What does increasing the temperature do to the next-token distribution, and why does that make outputs more varied?

Raising the temperature flattens that distribution, shrinking the gap between high- and low-probability tokens so the less likely candidates get a meaningfully larger chance of being sampled. interview.question: You claim attention scales better for training than RNNs. What property, absent in recurrence, makes that possible?
interview.model_answer: The key property is parallelism across positions: self-attention has no step-by-step recurrence, so every token's attention can be computed simultaneously rather than sequentially. interview.question: Given that self-attention is permutation-invariant, what role do positional encodings play, and what training benefit do they enable?
interview.model_answer: Self-attention treats its inputs as an unordered set, so without positional information the model cannot distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog.' interview.question: How does DPO differ from RLHF in terms of the reward model?
interview.model_answer: Classic RLHF is a two-stage process: you first train a separate reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimize the policy with an RL algorithm like PPO to maximize the reward model's scores. This removes the need to train and maintain a separate reward network and avoids the instability and complexity of running an RL loop like PPO. interview.question: As your agent takes multiple steps, why does appending the next observation preserve the cache while editing a previous turn does not?

interview.question: When a skill is triggered, what gets appended to the prompt, and what was in the prompt beforehand?

interview.question: How does an evaluation harness become more valuable as your agent is updated over time?
interview.model_answer: Each evaluation check you write keeps running against every future version of the agent, so its value compounds: a check added today protects you from regressions introduced by tomorrow's patches. Agent development is iterative, and fixes have a nasty habit of shifting behavior elsewhere — patching one failure can silently break something that used to work. A harness catches those behavior changes and regressions early, before they reach users, instead of leaving you in a reactive break-patch-break cycle. The trade-off is upfront cost: writing checks feels like overhead when the agent already works, but that cost buys a durable baseline. Without that baseline accumulated over time, you have no way to detect the regressions your own changes cause.

interview.question: When measuring an agent's efficiency, what concrete quantities would you actually track per run?

interview.question: What capabilities does span structure provide that plain flat log lines cannot?
interview.model_answer: Flat log lines are isolated text strings with no relationship to each other, whereas spans form a structured, causally-linked tree that captures each step's arguments, timings, and token/retry counts. Because a run becomes an inspectable tree of timed steps — planner, tool call, retriever, validator, final response — you can read transcripts and diagnose failures. With flat logs you'd have to reverse-engineer causality and structure by hand, and often the needed fields simply aren't there. In short, the linkage and structure are the raw material that makes evaluation and transcript-reading possible.

interview.question: What specific blind spots remain if you evaluate an agent only on static offline datasets?
interview.model_answer: Static offline datasets are reproducible, cheap, and safe to iterate on, but they can't see three things: real-world traffic, real users, and full-system effects. You never observe the actual distribution of inputs live traffic produces, so your test set may miss edge cases or drift. You also miss user-facing outcomes like satisfaction or conversion that only appear when real people interact with the agent. And you can't measure whole-system behavior under load — scale, latency, and integration failures — because offline runs isolate the model from the deployed system. That's why the principle is to start offline to gate changes cheaply, then graduate to online testing (A/B or shadow) to catch exactly what static data can't.
